newsitem.title: FRANCE: French judges accuse Chirac of interference.
newsitem.headline: French judges accuse Chirac of interference.

text.p: Senior French judges have accused President Jacques Chirac of forcing through the appointment of key law enforcement officials in a tussle over alleged cronyism, according to their report leaked to a newspaper on Wednesday.

The annual report by the independent Higher Magistrates' Council (CSM), obtained by the left-wing daily Liberation, followed charges that the ruling Gaullist RPR party is packing the judiciary to block embarrassing corruption probes.
The investigations involve alleged illicit funding of the party via kickbacks on public housing contracts while Chirac was mayor of Paris in 1977-95.

In the report to be presented to Chirac on Thursday, the CSM complained that its recommendations against certain appointments had been overridden in 46 percent of cases in 1996. "This is a break with past practice," it was quoted as saying.

Liberation said Justice Minister Jacques Toubon had tried to suppress the report, a severe embarrassment for Chirac, who called in January for reforms to guaranteee the independence of the judiciary and of public prosecutors.
The CSM said government intervention in nominations "fuels suspicion among judges and the public about the independence of the magistrates concerned from political authorities".
It recommended that the justice minister be stripped of his powers to order sensitive investigations pursued or shelved.

There was no immediate comment from the CSM or the Justice Ministry. Government officials say the president has overridden the CSM in only about four percent of all judicial appointments, but that is nevertheless nearly half of the instances where the CSM gave an unfavourable assessment of a candidate.
Liberation quoted a CSM member as saying that the ministry had sought to block publication of the report.

"No budget was allocated to the Council, there was a threat that it would be given no money to print the report...The authorities cannot accept these proposals which imply a strengthening of the CSM's powers," the unnamed member said.
Last July, the government filled the jobs of prosecutor at the Paris Appeals Court and the Supreme Court with Alexandre Benmakhlouf and Jean-Francois Burgelin, former aides to Chirac and Toubon.
In August, the government appointed a magistrate close to the Gaullist party as director of criminal affairs and pardons, a highly sensitive Justice Ministry position.

Benmakhlouf has under his control all the magistrates investigating alleged kickbacks at the Paris housing authority to feed Gaullist slush funds, the attribution of low-rent city-owned housing to relatives and political cronies and several other scandals involving the ruling parties.
Chirac appointed a panel of experts in January to propose reforms to better guarantee the independence of the justice system and protect the presumption of innocence.

The president sounded a note of caution on the central issue of cutting the umbilical cord between prosecutors and the justice ministry, saying the full implications of such a move needed to be examined thoroughly.
